container-queries.name: Container Queries
container-queries.desc: @container queries size components by their container, not the viewport — true component responsiveness.
container-queries.q: How do container queries differ from media queries? Why are they a big deal for design systems?
container-queries.qsub: What is a containment context and how do you set one up?
container-queries.what: Definition: Media queries look at the viewport; container queries look at the component’s own parent. Apply container-type: inline-size on the parent and write @container in the child.
container-queries.why: The same card component is used both in a sidebar (narrow) and the main area (wide). Media queries see the same viewport in both places, whereas container queries see the different container widths. This creates truly reusable components.
pros: Media query breakpoints par kam dependency
cons: Using container-type gives the element size containment (height can collapse)
gotchas: The container itself cannot query its own style, only its descendants can
With inline-size containment, width is not determined by the content
You need to consider fallbacks for older browsers
terms: @container (min-width: 400px) — the component changes style based on its container’s width.
Container query units — 1% of the container width.
where: card/media object adapts in every context.
the widget’s width changes within the grid.

media-queries.name: Media Queries
media-queries.desc: min-width/max-width breakpoints, feature queries, orientation, prefers-color-scheme / reduced-motion.
media-queries.q: How do media queries work? What does prefers-reduced-motion let you do?
media-queries.qsub: What is the difference between min-width and max-width breakpoint strategies?
media-queries.what:
Definition: @media is conditional CSS that applies rules based on viewport width (min-width/max-width), orientation, and user preferences (dark mode, reduced motion, contrast).

Modern syntax: min-width.
media-queries.why: The foundation of responsive design. User preference queries (reduced motion, dark mode) are essential for accessibility and polish — they’re not just about screen size.
cons: It is viewport-based, not component-based (container queries are the answer to this)
gotchas: Set breakpoints based on content breaking, not device names
Mixing max-width and min-width can cause overlaps/gaps
Hover-only interactions don’t work on touch devices — guard them with (hover: hover)
terms: Viewport width at which the layout changes — let the content decide, not the device.
Browser support check — not a media query, a feature query.

mobile-first.name: Mobile-First Strategy
mobile-first.desc: Base styles for small screens, layer up with min-width; why it produces simpler, faster CSS.
mobile-first.q: What does mobile-first mean in practice? Why is it preferred over desktop-first?
mobile-first.qsub: How does mobile-first reduce CSS overrides?
mobile-first.what: Definition: First write the layout for the smallest screen (default CSS, without media queries), then add complexity with @media (min-width) as the space grows.
mobile-first.why: On mobile, less CSS is parsed and there are fewer overrides. A single-column base is natural; expanding it on larger screens is easier than breaking a desktop layout down for mobile.
cons: Migrating an existing desktop-first codebase is work
gotchas: Mobile-first means using min-width, not max-width
Don’t forget touch targets (≥44 px) and the viewport meta tag
Don’t put desktop assumptions (hover, fixed widths) in the base styles
terms: Base CSS for the small screen, then layer on larger screens with min-width.
Basic experience for everyone, better features for capable devices.
Base for large screens, override for smaller with max-width — more overrides.

fluid-typography.name: Fluid Type & clamp()
fluid-typography.desc: clamp(min, preferred, max) for fluid font sizes and spacing without breakpoints.
fluid-typography.q: How does clamp() work? Write a fluid font-size that scales between 16px and 24px.
fluid-typography.qsub: Why is clamp() often better than a stack of media queries for typography?
fluid-typography.what: Definition: The clamp(1rem, 0.8rem + 1vw, 1.5rem) scales the font smoothly with the viewport, but never smaller than 1rem or larger than 1.5rem.
fluid-typography.why: Instead of typography that jumps at breakpoints, you get smooth scaling on a single line, and fewer media queries. The same technique works for spacing.
cons: Calculating values is a bit tricky (tools help)
gotchas: Using only vw prevents user zoom from working — mix rem + vw
If you write min > max, the min value wins
A very large max can ruin line length
terms: Keeps the value between min and max; val grows with the viewport.
Font/spacing continuously scale, without jumps at breakpoints.
Using only vw for font size breaks zoom — mix with rem.

flexbox.name: Flexbox — Main/Cross Axis
flexbox.desc: flex container vs items, main/cross axis, justify-content, align-items, align-content, flex-direction.
flexbox.q: Explain the flexbox axes. How do justify-content and align-items differ?
flexbox.qsub: How do you vertically and horizontally center a single element with flexbox?
flexbox.what:
Definition: Flexbox is a layout system that aligns and spaces items in a single dimension (row or column). Apply display:flex to the container; flex-direction determines the main axis.

justify-content = main axis, align-items = cross axis, gap = spacing between items, flex-wrap = wrap onto a new line.
flexbox.analogy: Bookshelf analogy: books on a shelf— the shelf runs in one direction (main axis), aligning the height of the books is the cross axis.
flexbox.why: Navbar, toolbar, card rows and similar 1-D layouts become much easier than using floats/inline-block: equal heights, centering, space-between—all in a single line.
cons: Grid is better for 2D layouts (both rows and columns)
gotchas: In flex-direction: column, the roles of justify and align are reversed.
Flex items have a default min-width:auto— long text can overflow; set min-width:0.
align-content works only on multi-line (wrapped) containers
terms: The line of the flex direction (horizontal in a row). justify-content works on this.
Perpendicular to the main axis. align-items works on this.
display:flex parent; its direct children become flex items.
where: Responsive rows using gap and wrap.

flex-items.name: flex-grow / shrink / basis
flex-items.desc: The flex shorthand; how items distribute free space; flex-basis vs width; flex:1 meaning.
flex-items.q: What does flex: 1 expand to and what does it actually do?
flex-items.qsub: What is the difference between flex-basis and width?
flex-items.what:
Definition: flex: grow shrink basis is a shorthand. flex: 1 = 1 1 0 — equal share. flex: none = no grow, no shrink. flex: 0 0 200px = fixed 200 px.

First the flex-basis sets the starting size, then any remaining (or deficit) space is divided according to the grow/shrink ratios.
flex-items.why: Keeping a sidebar fixed and giving the content the remaining space (flex:1) is the most common pattern. Without understanding shrink, items can stick together or overflow.
cons: Interaction between flex-basis and width can be confusing
gotchas: flex-basis overrides width (when not auto).
The basis of flex:1 is 0, so content size is ignored.
If a long word/URL overflows, use min-width:0 or overflow-wrap.
terms: How much of the free space to take (ratio).
How much to shrink when space is reduced.
Item's starting size before grow/shrink (higher priority than width).

grid-basics.name: CSS Grid — Tracks & Placement
grid-basics.desc: grid-template-columns/rows, fr unit, repeat(), gap, minmax(), auto-fit vs auto-fill.
grid-basics.q: When would you choose Grid over Flexbox? Explain fr and minmax().
grid-basics.qsub: What is the difference between auto-fit and auto-fill in repeat()?
grid-basics.what: Definition: CSS Grid is a 2D layout: rows and columns. Apply display:grid to the container and define tracks with grid-template-columns/rows; items automatically occupy cells. gap is the spacing between tracks.
grid-basics.why: For a responsive card grid, one line is enough: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(220px, 1fr)) — the number of columns changes with the screen size without media queries.
pros: 2D control; aligning and spanning items is easy
cons: Flex is simpler for small 1D layouts
gotchas: fr units don’t shrink below min-content; use minmax(0,1fr) to prevent overflow.
The difference between auto-fit and auto-fill appears when there are fewer items than tracks.
Implicit rows are controlled with grid-auto-rows.
terms: Minimum and maximum size of a track — minmax(200px, 1fr).
With repeat(), create as many tracks as fit; auto-fit collapses empty tracks.

grid-areas.name: Grid Template Areas & Line Placement
grid-areas.desc: Named grid-template-areas, grid-column/row line placement, spanning, implicit vs explicit grid.
grid-areas.q: How do grid-template-areas work? When are they clearer than line-based placement?
grid-areas.qsub: What is the implicit grid and how does grid-auto-flow affect it?
grid-areas.what:
Definition: grid-template-areas assigns names to layout regions, and items use grid-area: name. Alternatively, placement can use line numbers/span: grid-column: 1 / span 2.

An explicit grid is the one defined in the template; extra items go into implicit tracks.
grid-areas.why: You can reorder page layouts (header, sidebar, main, footer) in a media query simply by changing the template string—no need to modify the HTML order.
cons: If visual order differs from DOM order, it can confuse keyboard navigation or screen readers.
gotchas: Areas must be rectangular—L-shapes are not allowed.
Visual reordering does not change tab order (accessibility).
Line numbers start at 1, which is one more than the track count.
terms: Naming layout regions like ASCII art—easy to read.
grid-column: 1 / 3 — span an item using line numbers.
Tracks that were not defined but are created because of content.

responsive-images.name: Responsive Images (srcset / sizes)
responsive-images.desc: Serving right-sized images per viewport/DPR, sizes attribute, <picture> for art direction, aspect-ratio.</picture>
responsive-images.q: How do you avoid shipping a 2000px image to a phone? Explain srcset + sizes.
responsive-images.qsub: How does the aspect-ratio property help prevent layout shift for images?
responsive-images.what: Definition: srcset + sizes lets the browser choose the best image based on viewport and DPR; <picture> provides a different crop or format; CSS max-width:100%; height:auto and aspect-ratio keep the image fluid.
responsive-images.why: A correctly sized image greatly benefits both LCP and data. If sizes is wrong, the browser picks the wrong (large) image — the most common mistake.
cons: Multiple image variants need to be generated/hosted (doesn't work without a CDN/build tool)
gotchas: Write sizes based on the image’s layout width, not the viewport width.
Width/height or aspect-ratio without the image causes CLS.
object-fit crops the image, it does not stretch.
terms: The actual width of each candidate: img-800.jpg 800w.
Tells the browser how wide the image will appear in the layout, so it selects the correct candidate.
Reserves space before the image loads with aspect-ratio: 16/9 (prevents CLS).

viewport-units.name: Viewport Units & Mobile Gotchas
viewport-units.desc: vw/vh/vmin/vmax, the mobile 100vh address-bar problem, dvh/svh/lvh dynamic units.
viewport-units.q: Why does 100vh behave badly on mobile browsers, and how do dvh/svh fix it?
viewport-units.qsub: When would you use vmin or vmax?
viewport-units.what:
Definition: vw/vh are viewport-relative. On mobile the address bar hides and shows on scroll, so 100vh assumes a fixed (large) viewport and content can hide under the bar.

Fix: dvh (dynamic, changes with the bar), svh (always safe, small), lvh (with the bar removed).
viewport-units.why: The 'cut off at the bottom' bug on mobile for full-screen hero sections or bottom-fixed buttons occurs because of this. The modern solution is dvh.
cons: Layout can resize on address-bar scroll when using dvh
gotchas: 100vw includes the vertical scrollbar — horizontal scroll may appear.
dvh can cause jitter during animation/resize; svh is safer.
Write a vh fallback first for older browsers.
terms: Small / large / dynamic viewport height — based on the mobile address bar.
1% of the smaller or larger dimension.

typography.name: Typography Control
typography.desc: font shorthand, line-height, letter-spacing, font stacks/fallbacks, web-safe fonts, text-wrap: balance.
typography.q: What makes body text readable? Talk about line-height, measure, and font fallbacks.
typography.qsub: What does a good font-family fallback stack look like and why?
typography.what: Definition: Levers for readable typography: font-family stack, font-size, line-height (body text ~1.5), letter-spacing, max-width in ch (45–75 characters), and text-wrap (balance for headings, pretty for paragraphs).
typography.why: Typography makes up about 90% of the UI. Small line-height, very long lines, or wrong fallback fonts hurt both readability and CLS.
cons: Custom fonts load with a layout-shift trade-off (manage with font-display)
gotchas: Keep line-height: 1.5 unitless — pixel/em line-height inheritance can be wrong.
Both font-size and font-family are required in the font shorthand.
Very small (<16px) text can trigger zoom on mobile (on inputs).
terms: Unitless value (1.5) is best — it scales with font-size.

overflow-ellipsis.name: Overflow & Text Truncation
overflow-ellipsis.desc: overflow visible/hidden/scroll/auto, single-line ellipsis, multi-line line-clamp.
overflow-ellipsis.q: How do you truncate a single line of text with an ellipsis? What about multi-line?
overflow-ellipsis.qsub: Why does text-overflow: ellipsis require white-space and overflow to also be set?
overflow-ellipsis.what: Definition: For a single-line ellipsis, use three properties together: white-space: nowrap; overflow: hidden; text-overflow: ellipsis. For multi-line, use line-clamp.
overflow-ellipsis.why: Long titles in cards and lists break the layout. Proper truncation is a common machine-coding and interview question. Flex children also need min-width:0.
cons: Content is hidden — you need to provide a tooltip/expand to show the full text
gotchas: Flex items need min-width: 0 for ellipsis.
text-overflow requires overflow (hidden).
overflow: hidden can clip sticky positioning or box-shadow.

pseudo-classes.name: Pseudo-classes (:hover, :focus, :nth-child)
pseudo-classes.desc: State selectors, structural pseudo-classes, :focus-visible vs :focus, :not(), functional pseudo-classes.
pseudo-classes.q: What is the difference between :focus and :focus-visible? Why does it matter for accessibility?
pseudo-classes.qsub: How would you style every third item in a list?
pseudo-classes.what: Definition: Pseudo-classes select an element's state or position: :hover, :focus-visible, :checked, :disabled, :nth-child(), :not(), :has().
pseudo-classes.why: State styling can be done without JS. :focus-visible is essential for accessibility (do not remove the outline); :has() makes parent-based rules like “if this card contains an image, use a different layout” possible.
cons: Complex pseudo-class chains increase specificity
gotchas: :focus also applies on mouse click; :focus-visible applies on keyboard navigation
:nth-child counts all siblings, not just the same type ( :nth-of-type is different )
Hover-only UI does not work on touch devices
terms: Focus ring appears only on keyboard navigation — not on mouse click.
Exclude elements; :has() works like a parent selector.

pseudo-elements.name: Pseudo-elements (::before / ::after)
pseudo-elements.desc: Generated content, the content property, decorative shapes, icons, and layout tricks.
pseudo-elements.q: What is the difference between a pseudo-class and a pseudo-element?
pseudo-elements.qsub: Give a practical use of ::before or ::after you have actually used.
pseudo-elements.what: Definition: ::before/::after create a virtual child before/after an element's content. They require a content value (use "" for empty). Used for decorative icons, underline effects, clearfix, overlays.
pseudo-elements.why: Decoration without extra HTML elements. However, do not place meaningful content (text the user needs to read) in a pseudo-element — screen readers and copy-paste are unreliable.
cons: Not accessible via JS, and accessibility is limited
gotchas: Without content, ::before does not render
Pseudo-elements do not work on replaced elements (img, input)
Do not put important text in a pseudo-element
terms: Generated content inside the element; content property is required.
Styles input placeholders and selected text.
Give an empty string to create a decorative shape box.
where: a gradient/dim layer on top of a card.

backgrounds-gradients.name: Backgrounds & Gradients
backgrounds-gradients.desc: background shorthand, multiple backgrounds, linear/radial/conic gradients, background-size/position.
backgrounds-gradients.q: How do you layer multiple backgrounds? What is the difference between cover and contain?
backgrounds-gradients.qsub: How would you create a subtle striped background with a single gradient?
backgrounds-gradients.what: Definition: The background shorthand includes color, image, position, size, repeat. Gradients are background-image. Multiple backgrounds stack from top to bottom (the first is on top).
backgrounds-gradients.why: Gradients and multiple backgrounds create rich visuals without image files, keeping assets small and fast. Combining a gradient with an image is common for text overlays.
cons: Writing and debugging complex gradients is difficult
gotchas: Background images have no alt text — use <img> for meaningful images
In the shorthand, size follows the position separated by /
Gradients cannot be transitioned directly (use @property or an opacity trick)
terms: cover (fills the area, may crop) vs contain (fits entirely).
Multiple layers separated by commas: background: url(a), linear-gradient(...).
where: image + dark gradient for text contrast.

shadows-radius.name: Borders, Radius & Shadows
shadows-radius.desc: border-radius, box-shadow (inset, spread), drop-shadow filter vs box-shadow, outline vs border.
shadows-radius.q: What is the difference between box-shadow and filter: drop-shadow? When does each matter?
shadows-radius.qsub: Why should you never remove focus outlines without providing an alternative?
shadows-radius.what: Definition: border-radius rounds corners (50% = circle). box-shadow creates a shadow behind the element's box; multiple shadows are comma-separated. outline is like a border but does not affect layout.
shadows-radius.why: Shadows convey elevation (cards, modals). Layered soft shadows give better depth than flat design. Use an outline for focus indicators; do not use outline:none.
pros: Outline does not cause layout shift
cons: Large-blur shadows can be paint-expensive when animated
gotchas: box-shadow follows the element's box shape, not the shape of a transparent PNG (use drop-shadow for that)
Animating shadows triggers repaint — using an ::after opacity trick is better
outline: none without a replacement is an accessibility bug
terms: x y blur spread color; inset for inner shadow.
Shadow based on the element's actual shape (transparent PNG/SVG).
Outline does not take layout space and is for focus rings.

critical-render-path.name: Critical Rendering Path
critical-render-path.desc: DOM + CSSOM → render tree → layout → paint → composite; render-blocking CSS/JS; how the browser paints.
critical-render-path.q: Walk me through how the browser turns HTML and CSS into pixels on screen.
critical-render-path.qsub: Why is CSS render-blocking, and how do you reduce that cost?
critical-render-path.what: Definition: Browser creates DOM from HTML, CSSOM from CSS, combines both into render tree, then layout (positions/sizes), paint (pixels), composite (layers). CSS is render-blocking; synchronous JS is parser-blocking and also waits on CSSOM.
critical-render-path.why: First paint occurs when the render tree is ready. Inlining critical CSS, deferring or lazy-loading the rest, and using defer scripts improve FCP/LCP.
pros: Targeted optimization by understanding the rendering pipeline
cons: Maintaining critical CSS requires extra tooling
gotchas: Synchronous script pauses until CSS download completes
@import creates a CSS waterfall
Large CSS files block the entire page
terms: Combined DOM + CSSOM; only visible nodes.
CSS (and sync JS) prevent the page's first paint.
Extract geometry, fill pixels, combine layers on the GPU.
where: critical CSS inline for fast FCP.
Find blocking resources with Lighthouse / DevTools.

reflow-repaint.name: Reflow vs Repaint vs Composite
reflow-repaint.desc: Layout (reflow) recalculates geometry; paint fills pixels; composite layers GPU-blend. Which props trigger which.
reflow-repaint.q: What is the difference between reflow, repaint, and composite? Which is most expensive?
reflow-repaint.qsub: Give three property changes that force a reflow and three that only repaint.
reflow-repaint.what:
Definition: When a property changes, the browser does work: layout (width, margin, font-size, top) → paint → composite. Paint-only: color, background, box-shadow. Composite-only: transform, opacity.

If layout changes, paint and composite also occur.
reflow-repaint.why: The fewer stages are triggered, the cheaper it is. That's why animations are done with transform/opacity and the DOM isn't read/written again and again.
pros: Understanding the pipeline is the foundation for optimization
cons: You need to remember the list of properties (e.g., csstriggers references)
gotchas: A small layout change can affect an entire subtree
display:none removes layout, visibility:hidden does not
Reading layout properties in JS (e.g., offsetHeight) forces a reflow
terms: Combines layers on the GPU — cheapest.

layout-thrash.name: Layout Thrashing & Batching
layout-thrash.desc: Forced synchronous layout from read-after-write in JS; batching reads then writes; requestAnimationFrame.
layout-thrash.q: What is layout thrashing? How do you avoid forced synchronous layout in a loop?
layout-thrash.qsub: Which DOM reads force a synchronous layout flush?
layout-thrash.what: Definition: Layout thrashing occurs when a loop alternates reads (offsetHeight) and writes (style.height = ...) — each read forces the browser to recompute layout.
layout-thrash.why: In a loop over 100 elements, 100 layouts happen; if you batch the reads, only 1. This is the most common cause of 'animation/measuring with JS causes jank'.
pros: Large speedup from a small code change
cons: Code structure becomes slightly rigid
gotchas: getBoundingClientRect, scrollTop, offsetHeight can all trigger forced layout
ResizeObserver/IntersectionObserver polling is better
Avoid mixing reads and writes inside effects even in frameworks
terms: Reading a layout property immediately after changing style forces the browser to perform layout immediately.
Do all reads first, then all writes.
Schedule visual updates before the next frame.
codeSwap: // thrash: har iteration mein read + write
// thrash: read + write in every iteration

web-vitals.name: Core Web Vitals (LCP / CLS / INP)
web-vitals.desc: Largest Contentful Paint, Cumulative Layout Shift, Interaction to Next Paint; targets and common fixes.
web-vitals.q: What are the Core Web Vitals and what causes a poor score in each?
web-vitals.qsub: How would you diagnose and fix a high CLS on a page?
web-vitals.what:
Definition: Core Web Vitals are three real-user experience metrics: LCP (loading), CLS (visual stability), INP (responsiveness; replaces FID).

Fixes: preload/optimize LCP images, provide width/height and font fallback for CLS, break up long tasks for INP.
web-vitals.why: These are also Google search ranking signals and are directly tied to conversion. Lab data (Lighthouse) and field data (CrUX) can differ; real users' data is the field data.
cons: Collecting field data (RUM) requires separate effort
gotchas: Do not lazy-load the LCP image
Late-loading ads/banners/fonts increase CLS
Lab score can be good while field INP is poor
terms: Largest Contentful Paint — when the largest content is shown (target ≤ 2.5 s).
Cumulative Layout Shift — how much the layout moves (target ≤ 0.1).
Interaction to Next Paint — how quickly the screen updates after a click/tap (target ≤ 200 ms).
where: LCP image and CLS where conversions are sensitive.

/* the ratio comes from the width/height attrs */

font-loading.name: Web Font Loading (FOUT / FOIT)
font-loading.desc: font-display swap/optional, preloading fonts, fallback metrics, layout shift from font swaps.
font-loading.q: What is the difference between FOUT and FOIT? How does font-display control it?
font-loading.qsub: How do you prevent a layout shift when a web font finishes loading?
font-loading.what: Definition: Until the web font finishes loading, the browser either hides the text (FOIT) or displays it with a fallback font (FOUT). font-display: swap shows the fallback immediately and swaps when the font arrives; optional uses the font only if it is already in cache (no shift).
font-loading.why: Font swap changes the text width and causes layout shift (CLS). Preloading plus a size-adjusted fallback (size-adjust, ascent-override) reduces the shift.
pros: Text appears quickly, shift is reduced
cons: Deriving perfect fallback metrics is a bit of work
gotchas: The crossorigin attribute is required in font preload, otherwise the font may be downloaded twice
Don’t load too many weights/variants
Variable fonts save file size
terms: Flash of Unstyled Text — fallback font appears, then swaps.
Flash of Invisible Text — text is hidden until the font arrives.

css-containment.name: CSS Containment & content-visibility
css-containment.desc: contain property, content-visibility: auto to skip offscreen rendering, performance isolation.
css-containment.q: What does content-visibility: auto do for a long page?
css-containment.qsub: What kinds of containment does the contain property offer?
css-containment.what: Definition: The contain property gives the browser a hint that changes inside the element will not affect outside layout/paint, allowing it to isolate the work. content-visibility: auto skips layout/paint for off-screen sections.
css-containment.why: On long pages (feeds, articles) the initial render time can be dramatically reduced. Without contain-intrinsic-size, skipped content has a height of 0, causing the scrollbar jump.
pros: Initial render and scroll cost are lower
cons: Incorrect intrinsic size causes scrollbar jump
gotchas: The contain: size property prevents the element’s size from being derived from its content — provide an explicit size
Content skipped by content-visibility is still shown in find-in-page but remains in the accessibility tree
Measure before applying it everywhere
terms: Tell the browser that changes in the subtree do not affect the outside: layout, paint, size, style.
Skip rendering of off-screen content, render on scroll.
Placeholder size for skipped content (to prevent scrollbar jump).

naming-bem.name: Naming Methodologies (BEM)
naming-bem.desc: BEM block__element--modifier, why naming conventions fight specificity and scale in large codebases.
naming-bem.q: What problem does BEM solve? How does it keep specificity flat?
naming-bem.qsub: What are the trade-offs of BEM versus utility-first CSS?
naming-bem.what: Definition: BEM (Block__Element--Modifier) is a naming convention: .block__element--modifier. The class name itself indicates which component it belongs to.
naming-bem.why: In global CSS, name collisions and specificity wars occur. BEM provides flat, single-class selectors that stay at the same specificity, making overrides predictable. Drawback: long class names.
cons: Verbose class names
Deep nesting makes names very long
gotchas: Don’t create nesting like .card__title__link — flatten it
A modifier is never used alone; it is applied alongside the base class (card card--featured)
BEM is often unnecessary when using scoped CSS (modules)

css-modules.name: CSS Modules & Scoping
css-modules.desc: Locally scoped class names, hashing, composition; solving the global namespace problem.
css-modules.q: How do CSS Modules prevent class-name collisions? What does the build step do?
css-modules.qsub: How does composes work in CSS Modules?
css-modules.what: Definition: When a *.module.css file is imported, each class name becomes a unique generated name (card_3xK9a), so collisions are impossible. You use them via styles.card.
css-modules.why: The global namespace problem is solved without runtime cost (static CSS file). You get all the benefits of plain CSS: media queries, pseudo-classes, tools. For dynamic values, CSS variables are used.
cons: Dynamic styling (props-based) requires CSS variables or inline styles
Naming conventions are still needed (e.g., state classes)
gotchas: Global selectors (body, [data-theme]) need :global
Class names cannot be generated from dynamic strings — use styles['x']
Overriding a child component’s styles is difficult (use CSS variables)
terms: Class names are local to the file; the build tool generates a unique hash.
Reuse another class’s styles within a class.
:global(.x) when a global class is needed.

css-in-js.name: CSS-in-JS (styled-components / emotion)
css-in-js.desc: Runtime vs zero-runtime CSS-in-JS, dynamic styling from props, SSR concerns, performance trade-offs.
css-in-js.q: What are the pros and cons of CSS-in-JS? What is the runtime cost?
css-in-js.qsub: Why have zero-runtime solutions (Linaria, vanilla-extract) gained popularity?
css-in-js.what: Definition: CSS-in-JS writes styles in JavaScript together with the component (using template literals or objects). Runtime libraries inject CSS during rendering; zero-runtime tools extract static CSS at build time.
css-in-js.why: It provides colocation, dynamic styling, and automatic scoping. Drawbacks: runtime overhead, SSR/streaming complexity, and issues with React Server Components — so the industry has shifted toward zero-runtime solutions or CSS Modules/Tailwind.
cons: Runtime cost and bundle size
Friction with RSC / streaming SSR
gotchas: Don't define styled() inside component render — each render creates a new class
Extra setup is needed to prevent style flash (FOUC) in SSR
Ensure props don't leak to the DOM (use transient $prop)
terms: styled-components/emotion: styles in JS, CSS is injected at runtime.
Linaria/vanilla-extract/Panda: static CSS generated at build time.
Dynamic styles derived from component props.

utility-first.name: Utility-First CSS (Tailwind)
utility-first.desc: Utility classes, design tokens via config, purge/JIT, when utility-first helps or hurts maintainability.
utility-first.q: What is the case for and against Tailwind / utility-first CSS?
utility-first.qsub: How does Tailwind keep the shipped CSS small?
utility-first.what: Definition: In utility-first (Tailwind), you style HTML by applying small single-purpose classes instead of writing custom CSS. Configuration (theme tokens) provides consistent spacing and colors.
utility-first.why: No need for naming, no dead CSS, and the design system is enforced. Drawbacks: long class strings and the discipline required to extract components (reuse via React components, not @apply).
cons: Cluttered markup
Team needs to learn the conventions
gotchas: Dynamic class names (bg-${color}-500) get purged — write full class names
Extract very long class lists into components
Overusing arbitrary values breaks design tokens
terms: Defined in spacing/color config; utilities are generated from them.
CSS is generated only for the classes that are used.

theming-tokens.name: Design Tokens & Theming (dark mode)
theming-tokens.desc: Token layers, CSS variables for theming, prefers-color-scheme, per-component theming without JS.
theming-tokens.q: How would you architect a themeable design system that supports light/dark and brand themes?
theming-tokens.qsub: Why are CSS variables better than duplicated stylesheets for theming?
theming-tokens.what: Definition: Keep tokens in two layers: primitive (--blue-600) and semantic (--color-primary: var(--blue-600)). Changing a theme means remapping semantic tokens; components use only semantic tokens.
theming-tokens.why: Dark mode, brand themes, and high-contrast can all be handled by overriding CSS variables without a JS rewrite. The color-scheme property also themes native controls (scrollbars, inputs).
cons: Token naming and governance discipline required
gotchas: Flash of wrong theme: set the theme attribute before HTML loads (inline script)
Check contrast ratios in both themes
Don't write raw hex values in components — use tokens

preprocessors.name: Preprocessors (Sass) & @layer
preprocessors.desc: Sass nesting/mixins/functions, native CSS nesting, cascade layers (@layer) for predictable ordering.
preprocessors.q: What do preprocessors still offer now that CSS has variables and nesting?
preprocessors.qsub: What problem do CSS cascade layers (@layer) solve?
preprocessors.what:
Definition: Preprocessors like Sass gave CSS features that were not native (variables, nesting, mixins). Today CSS variables, nesting, @layer, color-mix() are native, so the need for a preprocessor is reduced.

Using @layer reset, base, components, utilities; determines ordering by layer order instead of specificity.
preprocessors.why: Cascade layers provide a structural solution to specificity wars: place third-party CSS in a lower layer and your styles in a higher one — they override without !important.
pros: Native nesting/variables keep the toolchain light
cons: Unlayered styles are always on top of layered styles — confusing
gotchas: The order of layers is determined by the first declaration
Layer order is reversed when using !important
Some things are still not native without Sass mixins/functions
terms: Variables, nesting, mixins, functions — compiled into CSS.
Cascade layers: the order of layers declared first takes precedence over specificity.

display.name: Display: block / inline / inline-block
display.desc: How elements flow: block (full width), inline (no box dimensions), inline-block (box + inline flow).
display.q: What is the difference between block, inline, and inline-block? Give a use case for each.
display.qsub: Why can you not set width/height on a pure inline element?
display.what:
Definition: display decides how an element will flow. div, p are block; span, a are inline; inline-block is a mix of both; none removes the element (also from the layout).

Today, for layout, most often flex and grid are used.
display.why: Issues like “my span’s width isn’t working” or “a gap appears below a button” are resolved by understanding the display model. The whitespace gap between inline-block elements also originates from this.
cons: Quirks such as inline-block gaps
gotchas: display:none also removes the element from the accessibility tree; opacity:0 does not
width/height are ignored on inline elements
elements with display:none cannot be animated or transitioned
terms: Takes the full width, starts on a new line; width/height/margin all work.
Flows within text; width/height are ignored, vertical margins have no layout effect.
Flows like inline but takes width/height like block.

margin-collapse.name: Margin Collapsing
margin-collapse.desc: Adjacent vertical margins collapse to the larger value; when it happens and how to prevent it.
margin-collapse.q: What is margin collapsing? Show a case where it surprises developers.
margin-collapse.qsub: How do you stop two vertical margins from collapsing?
margin-collapse.what:
Definition: When the vertical margins of block elements touch, they do not add; instead the larger one applies (20px + 30px = 30px).

This happens only in the vertical direction in normal block flow. Margins of flex/grid items do not collapse.
margin-collapse.why: This is an intentional feature so that spacing between paragraphs does not double. However, the surprise occurs when a child's margin-top pushes the parent down as well.
pros: Saves double spacing in vertical rhythm
cons: Surprising behavior when debugging layout
gotchas: Horizontal margins never collapse
Margins of flex/grid items and floats do not collapse
gap is a good way to avoid margin collapse
terms: Adjacent vertical margins do not add — the larger one remains.
Block Formatting Context — margins inside it do not collapse with outside margins.
The child's top margin escapes the parent if there is no padding or border in between.
where: Use flow-root to prevent unwanted collapse.

units.name: Units — px, em, rem, %, vw/vh, ch
units.desc: Absolute vs relative units; em (relative to parent font-size) vs rem (root); viewport and content units.
units.q: What is the difference between em and rem? When would you choose each?
units.qsub: Why can nested em values compound unexpectedly?
units.what:
Definition: Absolute: px. Relative: % (parent), em, rem, viewport units (vw, vh, dvh) and content units (ch, ex).

For font-size rem, for component-internal spacing em, for borders px is common.
units.why: When the user’s browser increases the default font size, the layout using rem scales accordingly; px does not — which benefits accessibility. ch provides a text-width limit (e.g., max-width: 65ch) that yields a readable line length.
cons: em nesting compounds — confusing
gotchas: The html { font-size: 62.5% } trick can break user preferences
em uses the parent’s font-size for font-size, but its own font-size for padding
100vh can be larger on mobile because of the address bar
terms: Relative to the root (html) font-size — predictable, best for accessibility.
Relative to the current element’s font-size (in padding/margin) or the parent’s (in font-size) — nesting causes compounding.
1% of the viewport width/height and the width of the '0' character.
where: rem for sizes; user settings respect.
em padding scales the component with the font-size.

css-variables.name: CSS Custom Properties (Variables)
css-variables.desc: --var declarations, var() with fallbacks, scoping/cascade, runtime theming, contrast with Sass variables.
css-variables.q: How do CSS custom properties differ from Sass variables? Why are they powerful for theming?
css-variables.qsub: How would you implement a runtime dark-mode toggle using CSS variables?
css-variables.what:
Definition: CSS custom properties --name are declared and used with var(--name). They are normal cascading properties, so they can be changed at runtime via selectors, media queries, or JavaScript.

Sass variables are replaced at compile time, so they cannot be used for runtime theming.
css-variables.why: Dark mode, theme switching, and component-level customization (--card-padding) happen without extra CSS. Change a variable with JS and the entire subtree updates.
cons: var() cannot be used in media queries (for breakpoints)
gotchas: If the value is invalid, the property becomes ‘guaranteed-invalid’ and the fallback does not apply unless you provide a fallback inside var().
Case-sensitive: --Brand and --brand are different.
For animation, you need to register the type with @property.
terms: Read the value with var(--brand, fallback), with a fallback.
The variable cascades/inherits — overriding it on an element affects its children.
where: Place tokens on :root, override on the theme.
--card-radius style knobs can be customized from outside.

positioning.name: Positioning — static/relative/absolute/fixed/sticky
positioning.desc: Normal flow vs positioned; containing block; offsets; sticky = relative until threshold then fixed.
positioning.q: Explain each position value. What is the containing block for an absolutely positioned element?
positioning.qsub: How does position: sticky decide when to stick, and why does it sometimes silently not work?
positioning.what: Definition: static (default, normal flow), relative (offset from its original position, space is still reserved), absolute (out of flow, positioned according to the nearest positioned ancestor), fixed (relative to the viewport), sticky (sticks on scroll).
positioning.why: Badges, tooltips, dropdowns and sticky headers are all created with positioning. The reason an absolute element appears in the wrong place is often that the parent does not have position: relative.
pros: Overlay and pin patterns are easy
cons: Absolute elements are out of flow — the parent’s height collapses
gotchas: If the parent has overflow: hidden/auto, sticky does not work
An ancestor with transform becomes the containing block for a fixed element
top is required for sticky; otherwise it never sticks
terms: Reference for an absolute element — the nearest positioned ancestor (relative/absolute/fixed/sticky).
Behaves like relative until the scroll threshold is reached, then sticks like fixed.

stacking-context.name: z-index & Stacking Contexts
stacking-context.desc: What creates a stacking context (position+z-index, opacity, transform), why z-index:9999 can fail.
stacking-context.q: Why can a z-index: 9999 element still appear behind another? Explain stacking contexts.
stacking-context.qsub: Name three properties (other than z-index) that create a new stacking context.
stacking-context.what:
Definition: A new stacking context is created when: the root element, position + z-index (not auto), opacity < 1, transform, filter, isolation:isolate, and many other cases.

Elements in different contexts are compared using the z-index of their parent contexts, not the children’s z-index.
stacking-context.why: z-index: 9999 fails because your element is inside a parent that itself resides in a lower stacking context. Fix: understand stacking contexts; increasing z-index alone will not help.
pros: Allows components to manage their own z-index internally
cons: Hidden contexts (transform, opacity) are difficult to debug
gotchas: opacity:0.99 or transform also creates a stacking context
z-index does not work on static elements (it works on flex/grid items)
Do not render a modal deep inside the DOM; use a portal
terms: An isolated layer group — the z-index of its children matters only within it.
Layer order of positioned/flex/grid items; compared only within its own stacking context.
isolation: isolate creates a new stacking context without side effects.

centering.name: Centering Techniques
centering.desc: Flex/grid centering, margin auto, absolute + transform, when each applies.
centering.q: Give me three ways to center a box both horizontally and vertically. Trade-offs of each?
centering.qsub: How do you center an element of unknown width and height?
centering.what: Definition: Centering depends on context: for text use text-align:center; for a fixed-width block use margin-inline:auto; for both axes use flex or grid; for overlays use position:absolute + inset:0; margin:auto.
centering.why: This is one of the most common interview questions. Today’s answer: display:grid; place-items:center. Older methods (absolute + negative margin, table-cell) appear only in legacy code.
cons: Context-dependent — a single method does not work everywhere
gotchas: Give the parent a height (e.g., min-height) otherwise vertical centering will not be visible
margin:auto requires a width on the block for horizontal centering
The absolute + transform method can produce blurry text
terms: Centers a block horizontally when its width is set.

float-legacy.name: Float & Clear (legacy)
float-legacy.desc: Historical layout with floats, clearfix hack, why floats caused collapsing parents.
float-legacy.q: What were floats originally for and why did they get abused for layout?
float-legacy.qsub: What is a clearfix and why was it needed?
float-legacy.what:
Definition: The original use of float was to wrap text around an image. In the 2000s it was hijacked for layout (columns), which required clear/clearfix hacks.

Today, flex/grid are used for layout; float remains only for image-text wrapping.
float-legacy.why: For reading legacy code and interview questions: floats are taken out of the flow, causing the parent’s height to become zero. This is called a “collapsing parent”.
cons: Fragile and hacky for layout
gotchas: Parent collapses when children are floated
clear works only on floats
Do not use float for new layouts — use flex/grid
terms: Move the element to the left/right side so that text wraps around it.
A hack that stretches the parent to the height of its floated children.

selectors.name: Selectors & Combinators
selectors.desc: Type, class, id, attribute selectors; descendant, child (>), sibling (+, ~) combinators; :is()/:where().
selectors.q: Explain the different CSS combinators with examples. What does :where() add over :is()?
selectors.qsub: What is the difference between .a .b and .a > .b?
selectors.what:
Definition: A selector indicates which elements the rule will apply to. Type (p), class (.card), id (#nav), attribute ([href^="https"]) and with combinators you can target precisely.

:is() and :where() compress repeated selectors.
selectors.why: The simpler and flatter the selector, the more maintainable and fast the CSS. Long descendant chains (.a .b .c .d) cling to the HTML structure — when the structure changes, the style breaks.
cons: Deep chains are fragile and increase specificity
gotchas: :is()'s specificity equals that of its most specific argument, while :where() has zero
Avoid the universal * and overly deep selectors
~ matches only later siblings, not the earlier ones
terms: The relationship between selectors: space (descendant), > (child), + (next sibling), ~ (later siblings).
They shorten selector lists; :where() has zero specificity.
where: Flat class selectors (.card, .card__title) are the safest.
Structural rules like h2 + p, article > p are suitable for prose.

specificity.name: Specificity & the Cascade
specificity.desc: How the browser resolves conflicting rules: specificity (id > class > type), source order, importance.
specificity.q: How is CSS specificity calculated? How would you resolve two rules fighting over the same element?
specificity.qsub: Where does !important sit in the cascade, and why is it a code smell?
specificity.what:
Definition: When two rules conflict on the same property, the browser first checks importance, then specificity (the count of IDs, classes, and types), and if there is a tie, the rule written later wins.

Think of specificity as a triple of (ids, classes, types): #a .b p = (1,1,1).
specificity.why: 80% of the answer to “Why isn’t my style applying?” is specificity. To avoid specificity wars (an !important over another !important), use low-specificity, flat selectors and @layer.
cons: Specificity wars make CSS ugly and broken
gotchas: No matter how many class selectors you chain, they cannot override an ID (classes are weaker than IDs, 11 classes != 1 ID)
!important can only be overridden by another !important — the chain becomes long
An inline style can be overridden only by !important
terms: Selector weight — inline > id > class/attr/pseudo-class > type/pseudo-element.
Origin/importance → specificity → source order (the later one wins).
Overrides the normal cascade; using it without a war is hard to justify.
where: Low specificity base styles + easy overrides.
Override library styles with @layer or a slightly more specific selector.

inheritance.name: Inheritance & initial/inherit/unset
inheritance.desc: Which properties inherit (color, font) vs not (margin, border); inherit, initial, unset, revert keywords.
inheritance.q: Which CSS properties inherit by default and which do not? How do you force inheritance?
inheritance.qsub: What is the difference between unset and revert?
inheritance.what:
Definition: Some properties (related to text) are automatically received by child elements. Box-related properties are not received.

Keywords: inherit (take the parent’s value), initial (spec default), unset, revert.
inheritance.why: Therefore, setting font-family once on the body applies to the entire page. And that’s why the font looks different on button/input — the browser gives them a default font, they do not inherit; you have to write font: inherit.
cons: You have to remember which property inherits
gotchas: all: unset also removes display — be careful
After inheritance, percent/em values become the computed value, not the original
Custom properties (--x) inherit by default
terms: unset = if inherited then inherit, otherwise initial; revert = back to browser default.
where: Set on body to cover the entire site.

box-model.name: The Box Model & box-sizing
box-model.desc: Content, padding, border, margin; content-box vs border-box; why border-box is the sane default.
box-model.q: Explain the CSS box model. What does box-sizing: border-box change and why do people set it globally?
box-model.qsub: A div has width:200px, padding:20px, border:5px. How wide is it in each box-sizing mode?
box-model.what:
Definition: Every element is a rectangle: content, padding around it, then border, then margin (the outer space).

box-sizing: border-box means width: 200px represents the whole box at 200px, including padding and border.
box-model.why: In content-box, width:100%; padding:20px exceeds the parent (100% + 40px). That's why almost every project applies a global border-box reset.
cons: Legacy/third-party CSS may assume content-box
gotchas: The margin is not part of the box and its background does not render
width: 100% plus padding overflows in content-box
Vertical margin/padding on inline elements does not affect layout
terms: Every element is a 4-layer box: content → padding → border → margin.
Default: width applies only to the content; padding and border are added on top.
width includes padding and border — predictable sizing.

transitions.name: CSS Transitions
transitions.desc: transition-property/duration/timing-function/delay, which properties are animatable, easing curves.
transitions.q: How does a CSS transition work? Which properties are cheap to animate and which are expensive?
transitions.qsub: Why does transition: all can be a performance foot-gun?
transitions.what: Definition: Transition property’s value automatically creates the intermediate frames when moving from one state to another. It occurs on a trigger state change (hover, class toggle). Syntax: property duration timing-function delay.
transitions.why: Small UI feedback (hover, open/close) does not require JavaScript. Choosing the right property is essential: transform/opacity remain smooth, width/height trigger layout.
cons: Only between two states; use keyframes for complex sequences
gotchas: transition: all can animate unexpected properties and degrade performance
display: none → block cannot be transitioned (now possible with transition-behavior: allow-discrete or @starting-style)
Cannot animate auto height (use a grid-template-rows: 0fr→1fr trick)
terms: Smooth interpolation when a property’s value changes: transition: opacity .2s ease.
A property whose value is continuous (color, transform, opacity). display normally is not.

keyframes.name: Keyframe Animations
keyframes.desc: @keyframes, animation shorthand, iteration, direction, fill-mode, play-state.
keyframes.q: How do @keyframes differ from transitions? When would you reach for each?
keyframes.what: Definition: @keyframes name { 0% {...} 100% {...} } creates a multi-step animation; we apply it to an element with animation: name 1s ease-in-out infinite alternate. It can run on its own without a trigger.
keyframes.why: Loaders, attention pulses, entrance animations and similar sequences cannot be created with transitions. Keyframes enable multi-step and looping animations in CSS.
cons: Less control with dynamic values (JS data); the Web Animations API is better
gotchas: Without animation-fill-mode: both the animation returns to the start state after finishing
Turn off infinite animations for reduced-motion users
Animation and transition on the same element can conflict
terms: Defines the animation steps: from/to or percentages.
forwards = the end state is retained; backwards = the start state during delay.
How many times: a number or infinite.

transforms.name: Transforms (translate / scale / rotate)
transforms.desc: 2D/3D transforms, transform-origin, why transforms do not trigger layout, will-change.
transforms.q: Why is animating transform smoother than animating top/left?
transforms.qsub: What does transform-origin control and when do you change it?
transforms.what: Definition: transform visually moves/scales/rotates/skews an element without changing layout (it stays in the same place relative to other elements). Order matters: translate() rotate() and rotate() translate() produce different results.
transforms.why: Transform skips layout and paint and runs directly on the compositor, so the animation is smooth (60fps). Animating left/top triggers layout — slow.
cons: Creates a new stacking context + containing block
gotchas: transform changes the containing block for children of a position:fixed element
It does not change layout space — overlap can occur
Do not apply will-change to everything; it consumes memory
terms: 2D transforms; now there are individual properties as well: translate: 10px.
The point around which rotate/scale occurs (default center).
Hints to the browser that this property will change — the layer may be promoted.

animation-perf.name: Animation Performance (compositor-friendly)
animation-perf.desc: Animate only transform & opacity to stay on the compositor; avoid layout/paint thrash; will-change budget.
animation-perf.q: Which two properties can you animate without triggering layout or paint, and why?
animation-perf.qsub: What does will-change do and why should you use it sparingly?
animation-perf.what: Definition: For smooth animation, animate only transform and opacity. These properties skip layout and paint and run on the compositor, whereas width/height/top/left trigger layout, and background/box-shadow trigger paint.
animation-perf.why: 60fps = 16ms per frame. Layout/paint happen on the main thread and compete with JavaScript; compositor animations stay smooth even when JS is busy. The DevTools Performance panel shows this.
cons: Layout-based animations (height: auto) need a workaround
gotchas: Do not apply will-change permanently
To animate a shadow, animate the opacity of ::after
Respect reduced-motion preferences
terms: transform and opacity animate on the GPU without the main thread.
Animating width, top, box-shadow forces layout/paint on every frame.
Only where needed; many layers consume memory.

semantic-html.desc: Using the right element for meaning: header, nav, main, article, section, aside, footer.
semantic-html.what:
Definition: Semantic HTML means selecting tags according to the content's meaning, not based on appearance. Use <nav> for navigation, <main> for primary content, and <article> for a standalone post.

Styling is CSS's job; the tag's job is to indicate what this element is.
semantic-html.analogy: Chapters, headings, and the index of a book. If everything is one big paragraph, no one can navigate. Semantic tags are the book's index.
semantic-html.why: Screen readers, search engine crawlers, and reader mode understand the page from the tags' meaning. <button> automatically gets keyboard (Enter/Space) activation and focus; <div onclick> requires you to add all that manually — and it is often forgotten.
pros: Better accessibility and SEO without extra work
Code is clear — the structure is evident just by looking at the tags
cons: New developers often get confused about when to use <section> versus <div>
gotchas: <section> without a heading is almost always the wrong choice — use <div> when you need a styling hook
There should be only one <main> per page
Do not skip heading levels (h1 → h4) — choosing a heading solely for size is wrong; change size with CSS
terms: A tag whose name itself describes its purpose — <nav>, <main>, <article>.
A large section of the page that a screen reader user can jump to directly.
Putting everything inside <div> — browsers and assistive technologies cannot understand anything.
where: <article> + heading hierarchy works well for both SEO and reader mode.
<main>, <nav>, <button> provide keyboard and screen reader support almost for free.

form-validation.what:
Definition: Validation can be done using only HTML attributes: required, minlength, pattern, min/max, type=email. The browser prevents submission and shows an error bubble.

For JavaScript, you have form.checkValidity(), reportValidity() and the input.validity object.
form-validation.why: For most basic validation, a library is not needed. However, client validation is only for UX — server-side validation must always be performed again because a user can bypass everything with DevTools.
pros: Accessible and localized error messages for free
cons: Error bubble styling is limited
Complex cross-field logic requires JavaScript
gotchas: Client validation is not a security measure — re-validate on the server
:invalid shows red on page load; use :user-invalid or a touched state
Adding novalidate disables native validation
terms: API to set a custom error message from JavaScript; an empty string clears the error.
Pseudo-class that shows the invalid state only after the user interacts (not on page load).
where: Most fields are covered with required + pattern + type.
Cross-field rules like “passwords match” using setCustomValidity.

forms-inputs.qsub: What is the difference between GET and POST form submission?
forms-inputs.what:
Definition: <form> collects user input and sends it to the server (action + method). Each field should have a name and a <label>.

Choosing the correct type opens the appropriate keyboard on mobile and the browser performs basic validation automatically.
forms-inputs.why: A placeholder is not a substitute for a label — it disappears as soon as you type and is not reliable for screen readers. Native forms get free Enter-to-submit, autofill, and password manager support; custom div-based forms break all of these.
pros: Better mobile UX with the correct type
cons: Customizing the native look is a bit difficult
gotchas: <button> default type is submit — give a non-submit button inside a form type="button"
A field without a name is not sent on submit
Don’t rely on a placeholder to act as a label
terms: <label for=id> or a label wrapping the input — clicking focuses the input and the screen reader reads the name.
The field’s key in a form submission is this; without a name the value is never sent.
email, number, date — appropriate keyboard on mobile and free validation.
where: type=email, type=password, autocomplete enables the password manager.
A GET form puts the state in the URL — shareable and back-button friendly.

media-elements.what:
Definition: Always provide <img>, alt, and width/height with loading="lazy". Use srcset + sizes for responsiveness; use <picture> for different crops/formats.

Include <video>, <audio>, and captions (controls) in preload / <track>.
media-elements.why: Images are the heaviest part of a page. Sending a 2000 px image to mobile wastes bandwidth. If width/height are not provided, the layout shifts as soon as the image loads (poor CLS).
pros: Browser automatically selects the best candidate
cons: Writing correct sizes is tricky — wrong sizes cause a larger image to be downloaded
gotchas: Don't apply loading=lazy to the LCP (hero) image
Provide width/height or aspect-ratio, otherwise layout shift
In alt text, don't write 'image of...'; describe the function
terms: Text substitute for the image — shown to screen readers and when the image fails. Use alt="" for decorative images.
Providing multiple image sizes to the browser so it can choose the appropriate one based on screen size and DPR.
Art direction — to show different crops or formats (AVIF/WebP) on different screens.
where: loading=lazy keeps the initial load light.

a11y-aria.q: What is the first rule of ARIA? When should you reach for aria-* attributes?
a11y-aria.what:
Definition: The first path to accessibility is semantic HTML. ARIA is needed only when a native element cannot do the job — such as custom tabs, comboboxes, live updates (aria-live).

ARIA only changes meaning; you still have to implement keyboard behavior and focus yourself.
a11y-aria.why: Incorrect ARIA, or not using ARIA at all, is even worse: if you add role="button" but don’t handle Enter/Space, a screen reader user will see a button but it won’t work. Hence 'native first, ARIA last'.
pros: Custom widgets are also usable for assistive technology
Icon-only controls receive an accessible name
cons: Misuse can cause problems; testing with a screen reader is required
gotchas: Do not apply aria-hidden="true" to a focusable element
role does not provide behavior — you must write keyboard handling yourself
If there is a visible label, use aria-labelledby or
terms: Accessibility attributes (role, aria-*) that give assistive technology extra meaning.
If a native element is available, do not use ARIA — <button> > div role=button.
When a modal/menu opens, move focus inside; when it closes, return focus.
where: focus trap, aria-modal and close with Esc; native <dialog> is best.
aria-live announces changes to the screen reader.

html-data-attrs.name: data-* Attributes & the DOM
html-data-attrs.qsub: When is a data attribute the wrong tool for holding state?
html-data-attrs.what:
Definition: data-* attributes store small custom data on an element that JavaScript reads via dataset and can be used with CSS attribute selectors ([data-state="open"]).

Values are always strings.
html-data-attrs.why: It is a simple way to connect server-rendered HTML to JavaScript or to expose state to CSS. But it is not a true state store — keep application state in JavaScript/framework.
pros: Context is directly in the markup, no extra lookup
Can be used by both CSS and JavaScript
cons: Values are strings; storing large data is inappropriate
gotchas: Do not store sensitive data in data-* — it appears in the page source
data-user-id → dataset.userId (kebab to camelCase)
Screen readers do not read data-* — use ARIA/semantic markup for meaning
terms: Custom attribute that starts with data- — for storing small extra data in HTML.
A stable way to capture an element for JavaScript or testing, separate from styling.
where: With data-action, many buttons can be handled by a single listener.
Toggle CSS using data-state/data-theme without classes.

script-loading.q: What is the difference between async and defer? Which would you use for a third-party analytics script?
script-loading.qsub: Why can a <script> in the <head> hurt First Contentful Paint?</head></script>
script-loading.what:
Definition: Normal <script> parsing stops. defer downloads in parallel and runs after the document is parsed, in order. async runs as soon as the download finishes, with no order guarantee.

type="module" scripts behave like defer by default.
script-loading.why: If the script stops the parser, the user sees a blank screen (FCP/LCP degrade). With the right attribute, the HTML displays first and the JS loads afterward.
cons: async scripts have unpredictable order — dependencies break
gotchas: Inline scripts are not affected by defer/async
Do not apply async to dependent scripts
defer scripts run before DOMContentLoaded
terms: The parser stops until the script is downloaded and executed, halting page rendering.
Parallel download, execute in order after HTML parsing.
Parallel download, execute as soon as download finishes — no order guarantee.
where: defer — runs in order when the DOM is ready.
async — does not depend on other scripts.
codeSwap: independent third-party (analytics): order ki parwah nahi -->
app code: order matters, DOM ready ke baad -->
app code: order matters, after the DOM is ready -->

html-doc-structure.q: Walk me through the essential contents of a <head>. Why does the viewport meta tag matter?</head>
html-doc-structure.qsub: What is the difference between placing a <script> in head vs end of body vs using defer?</script>
html-doc-structure.what:
Definition: The skeleton of every HTML page: doctype, <html lang>, <head> (metadata, not visible) and <body> (visible).

<head> contains charset, viewport, title, stylesheet links, and description.
html-doc-structure.why: If the doctype is missing, the browser switches to quirks mode and things like the box model behave in the old way. Without the viewport meta tag, the page appears tiny on mobile. The lang attribute lets screen readers choose the correct accent and gives hints to translation tools.
cons: You have to remember the boilerplate (frameworks/templates handle this for you)
gotchas: user-scalable=no should not be used — preventing zoom is an accessibility problem
The charset declaration should be within the first 1024 bytes, otherwise the browser may guess incorrectly
Place stylesheets in the and use defer on scripts — otherwise rendering is blocked
terms: <!doctype html> — tells the browser to render in standards mode, not quirks mode.
Informs mobile browsers to display the page at device width, not a zoomed-out desktop layout.
where: This boilerplate is needed without exception.
Titles, descriptions, and Open Graph meta create search and social previews.
